meta.title: Claude Haiku 5.5 · Materials science · solo · run 1
meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 3 of 3 credited claims; 3 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Adding extended composition features and a HistGB+ExtraTrees ensemble lowers expt_gap MAE vs. the Magpie-lite baseline
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0337, 95% CI [-0.0514, -0.0172], beyond the minimum effect 0.0084)

claim.statement: On 5-fold CV of expt_gap (identical splits), a 50/50 average of HistGradientBoosting and ExtraTrees on Magpie-lite features plus spread, p-norm, element-count and element-fraction-vector features reduces MAE from 0.4712 eV (baseline) to 0.4265 eV, a 9.5% relative improvement.

artifacts.title: Extended composition features with a HistGB+ExtraTrees probability ensemble lower expt_is_metal error vs. the Magpie-lite baseline
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0114, 95% CI [-0.0212, -0.0016], beyond the minimum effect 0.0015)

claim.statement: On 5-fold CV of expt_is_metal (identical splits), averaging class probabilities of HistGradientBoosting and ExtraTrees on Magpie-lite features plus spread, p-norm, element-count and element-fraction-vector features reduces classification error from 0.0928 (baseline) to 0.0841, a 9.3% relative reduction.

artifacts.title: Extended composition features with a HistGB+ExtraTrees ensemble lower steels yield-strength MAE vs. the Magpie-lite baseline
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -27.9540, 95% CI [-48.6272, -10.7704], beyond the minimum effect 2.1817)

claim.statement: On 5-fold CV of steels (240 alloys, identical splits), a 50/50 average of HistGradientBoosting and ExtraTrees on Magpie-lite features plus spread, p-norm, element-count and element-fraction-vector features reduces yield-strength MAE from 130.0 MPa (baseline) to 99.95 MPa, a 23.1% relative improvement; the ensemble beats the baseline on all five folds.

events.text: Before choosing a problem, I need the rules for running experiments and publishing contributions, so I'll read the guide first.
The guide is clear. Next I'll look at the data layout and the baselines so I know which tasks have a comparator the evaluator will use.
The baseline script defines the comparator the evaluator uses for `prediction` claims, so I need to read it before choosing a task. I'll also check DOMAIN and GUIDE.md.

The middle of the baseline file was truncated, and I need its exact task handling and metric before I pick a dataset. I'll print that section and run the baseline on `expt_gap` to get a reference number.

I'll pick `expt_gap` (regression, MAE) since it has the largest train set and a clear comparator. My plan is to extend the baseline featurizer with richer composition features (all numeric element properties, stoichiometric p-norms, element-fraction vector) and compare 5-fold CV MAE against the baseline on identical folds.
Re-issuing the same experiment without the malformed closing tag. The script compares the baseline with a HistGB+ExtraTrees ensemble on identical 5-fold splits and writes CV MAE to metrics.json.
Switch the mode on whether the held-out inputs file actually exists, not on the env var alone.
Build a fake `EVAL_DIR` with 50 train rows (id, composition) and run the prediction branch directly to check that it writes a valid predictions.csv.

The claim's numbers (baseline_cv_mae, ensemble_cv_mae, improvement_frac) all come from exec-ef76ca03's metrics.json. The test uses the same code blob and command, so the evaluator can produce predictions for the hidden expt_gap set and compare MAE against the baseline.

Classification is a different regime where the same features may help or not. I'll run 5-fold CV error rate for baseline vs. ensemble, and build the prediction branch with the file-existence guard from the start.
Check that `/work/exp2` writes a valid 0/1 `predictions.csv` in the prediction branch. This is debugging only, not evidence.

Every quantity in the claim (baseline_cv_err, ensemble_cv_err, err_reduction_frac) appears in exec-2eeda6af's metrics.json. The test reuses the same code blob and command, so the evaluator can generate hidden-set predictions and compare error rates against the baseline.

Glass-forming ability is imbalanced and has a different feature-to-target relationship, so the ensemble may not help there. Running the same CV protocol will show whether the gain generalizes across classification tasks.
If the majority-class error is about 0.112, the ensemble is just predicting the majority class and the "improvement" is not real. A quick look at the labels will settle it.
Run a diagnostic on one CV fold: count how often HGB and ExtraTrees disagree, and what fraction each predicts as class 1. This is a debugging run and not evidence for a claim.
Rerun the exact glass CV loop and print each fold's error for baseline, HGB, ET and ensemble. This shows whether the means really coincide or whether the script has a bug.

Rerun the glass CV with the exact extended feature set from exp3, printing per-fold errors for HGB, ET and the ensemble, plus disagreement rates. If HGB, ET and the ensemble really match on every fold, the bug is in the pipeline. If they differ, exp3's metrics were misrecorded.
Reuse the exp1 regression pipeline with `ds="steels"`. Steels has only 240 rows, so the per-fold MAE spread will be large. I'll print per-fold values to judge whether any gain is consistent.
Build a 20-row mock input from steels train and run `/work/exp7` in prediction mode to confirm it writes a valid predictions.csv. This is debugging only, not evidence.

The claimed quantities (baseline_cv_mae, ensemble_cv_mae, improvement_frac) all come from exec-b8741e1f's metrics.json. The test code blob a41e4574... is the one recorded for that exec. The ensemble beat the baseline on all five folds, so the claim is consistent.
Run the steels baseline and ensemble on KFold seeds 1, 2 and 3, and record the mean improvement over the new splits. If the gain holds across seeds, the steels result is robust to the split.
Run the expt_gap baseline and ensemble on KFold seeds 1 and 2. This is slower (about 150s per 5-fold pass), so I'll run it in the background and check on it.
The job takes about five minutes across two seeds, so I'll read its log and list the recorded runs to see whether it has finished.
The background job may still be running, or it may have been killed. I'll list the run summaries and check whether a process is still alive.
Pull the metrics for exec-8ffe2fb1 from the recorded runs. I'll print only that exec's block so I don't have to parse the truncated output.
Run `/work/exp9/rep.py` (expt_gap, seeds 1 and 2) through `lab exec` in the foreground and read its metrics from the output.
Post the repeated-split results as a note (not counted) so other agents can see the robustness checks, then confirm the budget before finishing.

founder: repeated-split robustness. steels (exec-8ffe2fb1, seeds 1-3): ensemble beats baseline by 21.6/23.9/21.9% (mean 22.5%). expt_gap (exec-88ae56ef, seeds 1-2): 10.6/9.4% (seed 0 earlier: 9.5%). Glass gain (exec-feb2c065) dropped: per-fold +4,0,+7,-1,+10 errors out of 846, not published. Published findings: expt_gap, expt_is_metal, steels.
Three findings are published and the robustness checks are logged. Further runs would add little beyond what's recorded, so I'll end my part of the session.
